## **4.3. Measurement Plan (KPIs)** {#4.3.-measurement-plan-(kpis)}

To validate the effectiveness of the CX Transformation Roadmap, we establish a two-tiered measurement framework. This ensures we track not only the final outcomes (Lagging Indicators) but also the immediate adoption of new initiatives (Leading Indicators), allowing for real-time adjustments.

The measurement plan is aligned with the three strategic pillars defined in the Solution Design phase.

### **4.3.1. Pillar 1: Physical Experience Metrics (The "Smart Lab")** {#4.3.1.-pillar-1:-physical-experience-metrics-(the-"smart-lab")}

Focus: Measuring Comfort and Operational Efficiency.

| Initiative | Leading KPIs (Activity/Adoption) | Lagging KPIs (Outcome/Satisfaction) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Smart Lab Ecosystem (HVAC & Zoning) | • Temperature Compliance Rate: % of operating hours the lab maintains 22-25°C. • Open Lab Utilization: \# of students accessing the lab during the new 4 PM \- 7 PM slot. | • Facility CSAT (Customer Satisfaction Score): Rating of lab comfort (Target: \>4.5/5). • Safety Incident Rate: Reduction in reported safety violations due to better visual zoning. |
| Digital Autonomy (Booking App) | • App Adoption Rate: % of students downloading and logging into the VNUK Lab Portal. • Booking Volume: \# of equipment requests processed digitally vs. paper. | • CES (Customer Effort Score): "How easy was it to borrow equipment?" (Target: \>6/7). • No-Show Rate: % reduction in missed bookings due to automated reminders. |

*Rational:* For Persona 1 **Thao Nguyen**, the critical success factor is the reduction of effort (CES) and the increase in physical comfort (CSAT).

### **4.3.2. Pillar 2: Cognitive Experience Metrics (Competence & ROI)** {#4.3.2.-pillar-2:-cognitive-experience-metrics-(competence-&-roi)}

Focus: Measuring Confidence and Employability.

| Initiative | Leading KPIs (Activity/Adoption) | Lagging KPIs (Outcome/Satisfaction) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Career Passport (Digital Badges) | • Badge Completion Rate: \# of students earning micro-credentials per semester. • LinkedIn Integration: % of students adding VNUK badges to their LinkedIn profiles. | • Employability Confidence Score: Survey asking "I feel prepared for the labor market" (Target: Increase by 20% YoY). • Part-time Placement Rate: % of badged students securing internal/external gigs. |
| Job Shadowing & Investor Report | • Participation Rate: % of Year 2 students completing the Shadowing Week. • Report Download Rate: % of students using the "Annual Growth Report" template. | • Industry Readiness Score: Rated by Alumni Mentors post-shadowing. • Parent NPS (Net Promoter Score): Likelihood of parents recommending VNUK (measured post-semester). |

*Rational:* For Persona **Khanh Chi**, the key metric is "Confidence" and tangible "LinkedIn Integration," proving that her tuition investment is yielding visible returns.

### **4.3.3. Pillar 3: Emotional Experience Metrics (Belonging)** {#4.3.3.-pillar-3:-emotional-experience-metrics-(belonging)}

Focus: Measuring Psychological Safety.

| Initiative | Leading KPIs (Activity/Adoption) | Lagging KPIs (Outcome/Satisfaction) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| BMS Buddy System | • Pairing Success Rate: % of Juniors successfully matched with a Mentor. • Interaction Frequency: Avg. \# of "Coffee & Cram" sessions attended per student. | • Sense of Belonging Score: Survey measuring "I feel supported by my peers." • Retention Rate: % of Year 1 students continuing to Year 2 (Target: 95%). |
| Anonymous SOS | • Engagement Rate: \# of questions submitted via Slido/Confession Box per week. • Response Time: Avg. time taken for TAs to answer SOS questions. | • Psychological Safety Index: Survey asking "I feel safe asking questions without fear of judgment." |

*Rational:* For Persona **Mai Anh**, the "Sense of Belonging" is the ultimate measure of success, ensuring she moves from isolation to integration.

### **4.3.4. Data Collection Methods** {#4.3.4.-data-collection-methods}

To ensure the KPIs are tracked accurately without overwhelming students with excessive surveys, we propose a Hybrid Data Collection Strategy. This approach combines automated system data (O-Data) with experiential feedback (X-Data) across three distinct channels.

#### **4.3.4.1. Automated System Telemetry (Passive Collection)** {#4.3.4.1.-automated-system-telemetry-(passive-collection)}

*Objective: To track leading indicators (Adoption & Compliance) without requiring student action.* Instead of asking students what they do, we will use technology to track their actual behavior.

* **The VNUK Lab Portal Logs:** The backend of the booking app will automatically record **Booking Volume** (number of requests), **No-Show Rates**, and **Peak Usage Hours**. This measures the adoption of the "Digital Autonomy" initiative.

* **IoT Sensor Data:** Smart thermometers installed in the laboratory will log temperature data every 15 minutes, automatically verifying compliance with the **"Smart Lab"** cooling standards (Target: 22-25°C).

* **Digital Badge Analytics:** Integration with LinkedIn/Credly will provide reports on how many students have successfully claimed and shared their **"Career Passport"** badges on social media.

#### **4.3.4.2. Transactional Micro-Surveys (Event-Triggered)** {#4.3.4.2.-transactional-micro-surveys-(event-triggered)}

*Objective: To capture immediate emotional reactions (CSAT & CES) at specific touchpoints.* These are "in-the-moment" feedback loops, designed to be completed in under 30 seconds.

* **The "QR Check-out":** A QR code placed at the exit of the laboratory. After a practice session, students scan it to rate their physical comfort (CSAT) on a 5-point scale using a simple emoji interface.

* **App Pop-ups:** Immediately after a student successfully books equipment on the portal, a pop-up asks a single question: *"How easy was it to book this tool?"* (Measuring Customer Effort Score \- CES).

* **Real-time Confusion Meter:** Usage statistics from **Slido/Mentimeter** during lectures will be exported weekly to measure the engagement level of the **"Anonymous SOS"** system.

#### **4.3.4.3. Periodic Deep-Dive Surveys (Strategic)** {#4.3.4.3.-periodic-deep-dive-surveys-(strategic)}

*Objective: To measure overall relationship health and long-term impact (NPS & Belonging).*

* **The "End-of-Semester" Voice of Student (VoS):** A comprehensive survey sent via email twice a year. This is the only "long-form" survey, focusing on:

  * **Net Promoter Score (NPS) (Reichheld, 2003):** *"How likely are you to recommend VNUK to a friend?"*

  * **Psychological Safety Index:** Measuring the impact of the **"BMS Buddy System"** and feelings of isolation.

  * **Career Confidence Score:** Self-assessment of employability to validate the effectiveness of the "Job Shadowing" and "Investor Report" initiatives.

5. # **ADVANCE Phase \- Embed & Evolve**  {#advance-phase---embed-&-evolve}

## **5.1. Recommendations for Organization Governance** {#5.1.-recommendations-for-organization-governance}

To ensure that this CX transformation is not just a one-time project but a lasting part of the BMS department, VNUK must move away from traditional, fragmented management. We need a governance structure that treats the student journey as a single, unified experience rather than a series of tasks handled by separate offices.

### **5.1.1 The Establishment of the VNUK CX Council** {#5.1.1-the-establishment-of-the-vnuk-cx-council}

The foundation of this governance model is the creation of a BMS CX Council. This is not merely another administrative committee, but a strategic body chaired by the Dean of VNUK and including the Head of Department, the Manager, and representatives from the Student Affairs, Academic Affairs and Career Offices. The primary role of this Council is to ensure that every operational decreatio \- whether it is a change in the curriculum or an upgrade to laboratory equipment \- is filtered through the lens of student experience. By meeting quarterly to review journey-specific data, the Council can ensure that the "Experience" phase of the student journey remains a priority, preventing the program from slipping back into a purely academic focus that ignores student emotions.

### **5.1.2 Closed-Loop Feedback and Operational Accountability** {#5.1.2-closed-loop-feedback-and-operational-accountability}

Governance must also provide a clear framework for managing the day-to-day delivery of "Quick Win" solutions. For instance, the BMS Buddy System and the 15-Minute Rule require consistent participation from senior students and faculty. The Council establishes accountability by appointing "CX Champions" within each faculty who monitor these interactions. If a solution like the Anonymous SOS System reveals a consistent friction point in the curriculum, the governance structure empowers the Academic Affairs department to intervene and adjust the syllabus immediately. This ensures that feedback is not just collected but is used as a trigger for the Closed-loop feedback mechanism, where individual problems are resolved quickly and effectively.

### **5.1.3 Standardizing Success through Shared KPIs** {#5.1.3-standardizing-success-through-shared-kpis}

Finally, the governance model must link the success of implemented solutions to the university's official performance metrics. To ensure that the Career Passport and Job Shadowing Program remain effective, the CX Council tracks "Market Readiness" indicators alongside traditional grades. This includes monitoring the adoption rates of digital badges and the quality of alumni-mentor connections. By embedding these journey-specific metrics into the department's annual reviews, VNUK creates a permanent incentive for staff to improve the ease and effectiveness of student interactions. This standardized approach to measurement ensures that the university can track its maturity as it moves from the "Ad-hoc" stage toward becoming a fully "Optimized" customer-obsessed organization.

## **5.2. Employee Engagement & Enablement** {#5.2.-employee-engagement-&-enablement}

The success of any Customer Experience (CX) transformation depends heavily on the people who deliver it. At VNUK, lecturers, laboratory technicians, and administrative staff are the primary "human touchpoints" in a student’s journey. According to the "service-profit chain" concept, engaged and empowered employees lead to satisfied students. Therefore, to move VNUK toward a student-centric culture, the institution must focus on enabling its staff with the right mindset, tools, and authority to resolve student pain points at the source.

### **5.2.1  Cultivating a Student-Centric Mindset** {#5.2.1-cultivating-a-student-centric-mindset}

The first step in employee enablement is ensuring that every staff member understands the human side of the student journey. Academic and non-academic staff often focus strictly on their functional duties \- grading papers or processing forms \- without fully realizing the emotional weight these tasks carry for the student. VNUK should implement "Empathy Workshops" where staff are introduced to the core personas identified in this roadmap. By understanding the specific fears and goals of different student segments, a lecturer is more likely to adopt supportive behaviors, such as the "15-minute rule," not as a mandatory task, but as a meaningful way to provide emotional reassurance. When employees see the direct impact of their actions on student success, their work gains a higher sense of purpose, which is a key driver of long-term engagement.

### **5.2.2 Empowerment and Autonomy at the Frontline** {#5.2.2-empowerment-and-autonomy-at-the-frontline}

Enablement also requires giving staff the autonomy to solve friction points at the source without waiting for layers of approval. This is particularly relevant for the Digital Autonomy & Trust initiative, where laboratory technicians and administrative officers should be empowered to resolve equipment booking conflicts or technical issues immediately. When frontline employees have the authority to act on their observations, they transition from being task-oriented workers to "Experience Owners." This sense of ownership directly supports the university’s transition toward Customer Obsession, as it encourages a proactive mindset where staff anticipate and fix problems before they escalate into "moments of misery" for the student.

### **5.2.3 Recognition and Skill Development** {#5.2.3-recognition-and-skill-development}

Finally, to sustain engagement, VNUK must align its internal recognition systems with the successful implementation of its CX solutions. Traditionally, academic staff are rewarded for research output; however, to evolve the culture, the university should introduce awards for "CX Excellence" based on qualitative feedback from the Closed-Loop Feedback system. Recognizing a faculty member for their outstanding mentorship in the Buddy System or an administrative staffer for simplifying a complex process reinforces the behavior we want to see. By providing professional development in "soft skills" like active listening and conflict resolution, VNUK ensures its team is emotionally and technically equipped to maintain the high standards of an international university.

## **5.3. Technology & Ecosystem Requirements** {#5.3.-technology-&-ecosystem-requirements}

For the CX Transformation at VNUK to be sustainable, the digital infrastructure must serve as a functional backbone that directly supports the solutions introduced in the ACT Phase. To move toward a "Student-Success-Centric" ecosystem, the university’s technology must evolve beyond basic data storage and focus on creating a seamless, integrated environment that reduces administrative friction and enhances personalized support.

### **5.3.1 Integrated Platforms for Operational Efficiency** {#5.3.1-integrated-platforms-for-operational-efficiency}

The primary technical requirement is the integration of fragmented data sources into a centralized ecosystem that supports the "Smart Lab" and "Digital Autonomy" initiatives. Currently, information is often siloed across different platforms, making it difficult to track a student’s progress holistically. By connecting the Learning Management System (LMS) with a centralized student database, VNUK can automate the "Closed-loop feedback" mechanism. For instance, when the "Anonymous SOS System" flags a recurring academic struggle, the system should automatically alert relevant faculty members, allowing for the proactive intervention necessary to maintain a supportive journey. This integration ensures that the digital tools developed are not just standalone apps but are part of a responsive institutional nervous system.

### **5.3.2 Digital Infrastructure**  {#5.3.2-digital-infrastructure}

The technology ecosystem must also provide the platform for professional validation solutions like the "Career Passport". VNUK requires a secure, industry-recognized digital badging system that integrates with professional networks like LinkedIn. Furthermore, to support the "Job Shadowing Program", the university needs a searchable alumni-mentor database that facilitates connections between current students and the professional market. These digital assets do not just provide convenience; they build the "Effectiveness" pillar of the CX strategy by giving students the physical and digital proof of competence they need to feel job-ready before graduation.

### **5.3.3 Scalable Insight Tools for Continuous Evolution** {#5.3.3-scalable-insight-tools-for-continuous-evolution}

Finally, the ecosystem requires scalable tools to manage the Voice of the Student (VoS) and institutional feedback loops. To move away from generic, low-response surveys, VNUK should implement micro-feedback technology, such as the "Real-time Confusion Meter", directly into the lecture and service environments. These tools provide the "Open-loop" strategic data needed by the CX Council to identify systemic trends and prioritize long-term infrastructure upgrades. By utilizing automated sentiment analysis on both solicited and unsolicited feedback, VNUK can detect "weak signals" of dissatisfaction early. This technological capability ensures that the university remains in a state of continuous evolution, where data-driven insights from the frontline are used to refine and scale solutions across all faculties.

## **5.4. Cultural Change Management** {#5.4.-cultural-change-management}

The final and perhaps most challenging step in the ADVANCE phase is the transformation of VNUK’s organizational culture. Implementing technical solutions like the “Smart Lab” or digital booking portals is ineffective if the underlying culture remains reactive and siloed. To achieve true Customer Obsession, VNUK must shift its collective mindset from "delivering an academic curriculum" to "orchestrating a student-success ecosystem". This cultural change requires a deliberate strategy that aligns individual behaviors with the university’s broader CX vision.

### **5.4.1 Shifting from Academic Silos to Journey Ownership** {#5.4.1-shifting-from-academic-silos-to-journey-ownership}

A primary goal of change management is to break down the functionistration- such as admissions, faculty, and adminnistration- that currently manage student interactions in isolation. Cultural transformation occurs when every staff member, from senior leadership to lab technicians, understands their specific impact on the end-to-end student journey. This requires moving away from a mindset where "student satisfaction" is the sole responsibility of a student services department. Instead, the university must foster a culture of "Journey Ownership," where every touchpoint is seen as a meaningful intervention for building the psychological safety and confidence students need to succeed. By communicating succennnnistration \- such as how early industry exposure improved student confidence \- leadership can make the abstract concept of "Customer Experience" tangible and rewarding for all employees

### **5.4.2 Establishing a "Safe-to-Learn" Internal Culture** {#5.4.2-establishing-a-"safe-to-learn"-internal-culture}

For students to feel comfortable in the “Safe Zone” environments proposed in the ACT phase, the staff must first model that behavior internally. Cultural change management at VNUK should encourage an environment where feedback is viewed as a strategic asset rather than a criticism. This involves normalizing the use of the “Closed-Loop Feedback” system among employees. When staff members see that identifying a friction point leads to support and resources rather than blame, they become more proactive in seeking out "Moments of Misery" to fix. This internal transparency is essential to sustain solutions like the “Anonymous SOS System,” as it ensures that the data collected actually leads to supportive academic adjustments rather than defensive administrative reactions.

### **5.4.3 Leadership Alignment and Symbolic Actions** {#5.4.3-leadership-alignment-and-symbolic-actions}

Deep cultural change must be led from the top through consistent, symbolic actions. Senior leaders act as the ultimate "CX Champions" by actively participating in the student journey themselves, such as attending project presentations or personally reviewing facility standards. When leadership prioritizes student-centric KPIs over traditional administrative metrics in public meetings, it sends a powerful signal to the entire organization about what truly defines success at VNUK. By celebrating small wins and acknowledging the effort required to change old habits, leadership builds the momentum necessary to move the university from an "Ad-hoc" maturity level to an "Optimized" state, where student success is permanently embedded in the institutional DNA.

6. # **Challenges, Risks & Contingency Plans** {#challenges,-risks-&-contingency-plans}

## **6.1. Financial Risks** {#6.1.-financial-risks}

The execution of the CX transformation roadmap may encounter several practical challenges related to financial resources, organizational operations, and technology readiness. From a financial perspective, CX transformation requires continuous investment in staff training, digital tools, and process improvement, which may create budget pressure, especially in the early stages when results are not yet visible. To manage this risk, the organization should prioritize CX initiatives that directly address critical customer pain points and demonstrate short-term value. A phased implementation approach and the use of pilot projects can help control costs and justify further investment.

## **6.2. Operational Resistance** {#6.2.-operational-resistance}

Operational resistance is another significant challenge, as employees may be reluctant to adopt new CX practices due to increased workload, unclear responsibilities, or limited understanding of the CX strategy. This resistance can slow down implementation and reduce the effectiveness of CX initiatives. To mitigate this risk, management should clearly communicate the CX vision, align CX objectives with employee performance metrics, and actively involve staff in CX-related activities such as journey mapping and service improvement workshops. Providing continuous training and leadership support is essential to embed a customer-centric mindset across the organization.

## **6.3. Technical Barriers** {#6.3.-technical-barriers}

Technical barriers represent a critical risk in executing the CX transformation roadmap, particularly due to the organization’s reliance on legacy systems and fragmented digital infrastructure. Existing systems may not be designed to support end-to-end customer journey management, resulting in disconnected touchpoints, duplicated data, and inconsistent customer information across departments. These limitations reduce the organization’s ability to deliver a seamless and personalized customer experience.

In addition, the lack of integrated customer data platforms can hinder effective CX measurement and decision-making. Without a unified view of the customer, it becomes difficult to track customer behavior across channels, identify pain points accurately, or evaluate the impact of CX initiatives. This may lead to delayed responses and suboptimal service improvements.

To mitigate these technical barriers, the organization should adopt a gradual and modular technology upgrade strategy rather than attempting a full system replacement. Priority should be given to integrating key systems, improving data consistency, and enabling basic customer analytics that support CX goals. Close collaboration between CX teams and IT departments is essential to ensure that technology investments directly support customer journey improvements and long-term CX capability development.

7. # **Conclusion and Reflection** {#conclusion-and-reflection}

## **7.1. The CX Wheel Blueprint Summary** {#7.1.-the-cx-wheel-blueprint-summary}

![][image20]

*BMS Students CX Wheel*

To transition VNUK from an "Ad-hoc" maturity level to an "Optimized" student-centric organization, our group has developed a phased transformation roadmap. This roadmap is structured into four strategic phases Aspire, Aware, Act, and Advance ensuring a systematic approach to elevating the Student Experience (SX).

**Phase 1: Aspire (Strategic Foundation)** The transformation begins by establishing a clear vision. In this phase, we defined the "Student-First" strategy and established the CX Steering Committee. This governance structure ensures that CX is not treated as a temporary initiative but is prioritized by senior leadership, setting the necessary direction and resources for change.

**Phase 2: Aware (Deep Understanding)** Moving beyond assumptions, this phase focuses on deep customer insight. By developing detailed Student Personas and conducting Journey Mapping, we diagnosed the critical pain points in the current student journey. This phase shifted the organization's perspective from an inside-out view (administrative-focused) to an outside-in view (student-focused), identifying exactly where the experience was breaking down.

**Phase 3: Act (Execution & Design)** Translating insights into tangible solutions, the "Act" phase deploys key initiatives to resolve friction. We proposed the implementation of the "One-Stop Hub" to unify support channels and the "Anonymous SOS System" to provide psychological safety. Concurrently, we established a Measurement Framework (NPS, CSAT) to replace sporadic surveys with real-time feedback loops, allowing for immediate service recovery.

**Phase 4: Advance (Cultural Integration)** The final phase ensures sustainability and continuous improvement. Here, the focus shifts to Culture and widespread adoption. By training staff as "CX Champions" and embedding student-centric KPIs into operational performance, this phase institutionalizes the changes, ensuring that the new Student Experience becomes the standard "way of life" at VNUK.

## **7.2. Learning Outcomes & Reflection** {#7.2.-learning-outcomes-&-reflection}

Undertaking the "CX Transformation Roadmap for VNUK" project has been a significant learning journey for our group, bridging the gap between academic concepts and real-world application. Through the process of analyzing and redesigning the student experience, we have achieved the following key learning outcomes:

From "Passive Users" to "Experience Architects": As students ourselves, we initially viewed VNUK’s issues through a subjective lens. However, applying the CX Wheel forced us to step back and adopt the objective mindset of a strategist. We learned that designing an experience requires more than just identifying problems; it demands a systematic approach to diagnosing root causes (People, Process, or Technology) and crafting viable solutions.

**The Power of Data-Driven Empathy:** Developing Student Personas and conducting Journey Mapping taught us that "you are not the user." We realized that assumptions are the enemy of effective CX. By validating pain points through data, we learned how to design solutions that address genuine student needs (such as psychological safety via the SOS system) rather than what we *assumed* they needed.

**Complexity of Service Ecosystems:** This project highlighted that Student Experience (SX) is not the sole responsibility of the Student Affairs department but a cross-functional effort. We gained a deeper appreciation for organizational interdependencies, understanding that a seamless "One-Stop Hub" requires tight coordination between IT, Academic Affairs, and Facilities management.

**Strategic Planning & Change Management:** Formulating the 4-phase roadmap (Aspire \- Aware \- Act \- Advance) helped us develop critical skills in strategic planning. We learned to balance ambition with feasibility, understanding that cultural transformation (Phase 4\) cannot happen without first establishing a strong operational foundation (Phase 1 & 2).

In conclusion, this project has equipped us with not only the technical tools of CX management (NPS, Journey Maps) but also the strategic mindset to drive human-centric change in any future organization we join.
